  .cl-seg button:focus-visible, .cd-seg button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--dm-t1); outline-offset: 1px; }
  .cl-loop { --vc: var(--st-ok); --gc: var(--st-ok); --g: .07; }
  .cl-loop[data-mode="block"] { --vc: var(--st-bad); --gc: var(--st-bad); --g: .81; }
  .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] { --vc: var(--st-ask); --gc: var(--st-bad); --g: .78; }

  .clp-fig svg.ft { display: none; max-width: 380px; margin: 0 auto; }
  .cl-loop .lb > rect { fill: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 8%, var(--dm-bg)); stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 62%, transparent); stroke-width: 1.4; }
  .cl-loop .lb.fz > rect { fill: none; stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 48%, transparent); stroke-dasharray: 5 4; }
  .cl-loop .lb.ex > rect { fill: none; stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 30%, transparent); transition: stroke .3s ease, fill .3s ease; }

  .cl-loop .la { fill: var(--dm-t1); font-size: 11.5px; font-weight: 500; }
  .cl-loop .le path { fill: none; stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 64%, transparent); stroke-width: 1.5; stroke-linejoin: round; transition: stroke .3s ease; }
  .cl-loop .le polygon, .cl-loop .lj { fill: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 64%, transparent); transition: fill .3s ease; }
  .cl-loop .le.e-fb path { stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 34%, transparent); }
  .cl-loop .le.e-fb polygon { fill: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 34%, transparent); }
  .cl-loop .le.e-opt path { stroke: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 42%, transparent); stroke-dasharray: 4 4; }
  .cl-loop .le.e-opt polygon { fill: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 42%, transparent); }
  .cl-loop .le.e-verdict path { stroke: var(--vc); stroke-width: 2; }
  .cl-loop .le.e-verdict polygon { fill: var(--vc); }

  .cl-loop[data-mode="exec"] .le.e-exec path { stroke: var(--st-ok); stroke-width: 2; }

  .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] .le.e-ask path { stroke: var(--st-ask); stroke-width: 2; }

  .cl-loop .lx circle { fill: var(--st-bad); stroke: var(--dm-bg); stroke-width: 2; }

  .cl-loop .m-exec, .cl-loop .m-block, .cl-loop .m-ask { display: none; }
  .cl-loop[data-mode="exec"] .m-exec, .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] text.la.m-exec, .cl-loop[data-mode="block"] .m-block, .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] .m-ask { display: inline; }
  .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] text.la.m-exec { fill: var(--dm-t2); }

  .cl-loop .lg-b { fill: none; stroke: var(--dm-t1); stroke-width: 1.5; }

  .cl-loop .w-sep { fill: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 45%, transparent); }
  .cl-loop[data-mode="exec"] .w-exec, .cl-loop[data-mode="block"] .w-block, .cl-loop[data-mode="ask"] .w-ask { fill: var(--dm-t1); font-weight: 700; }

  .cb-k2 { width: 18px; height: 6px; border-radius: 3px; background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 60%, transparent); }
  .cb-row, .cb-axis { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 9.4rem minmax(0, 1fr) 2.4rem; align-items: center; column-gap: .9rem; }
  .cb-row { padding: .3rem 0; }

  .cb-name small, .cr-name small { display: block; margin-top: .12rem; font-size: .68rem; font-weight: 400; color: var(--dm-t2); }
  .cb-track { position: relative; height: 50px; --c: var(--st-ok); }
  .cb-row.bad .cb-track { --c: var(--st-bad); }
  .cb-track::before { content: ""; position: absolute; left: calc(100% / 9); top: 4px; bottom: 0; border-left: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, .13); }
  .cb-now { position: absolute; left: -5px; top: 30px; width: 11px; height: 11px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--dm-bg); border: 2px solid var(--dm-t1); z-index: 2; }
  .cb-aft { position: absolute; left: calc(var(--v) * 1%); top: 30px; width: 11px; height: 11px; margin-left: -5.5px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--c); box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px var(--dm-bg); z-index: 2; }
  .cb-ret { position: absolute; left: 14px; right: calc(100% - var(--v) * 1%); top: 31px; height: 9px; border-radius: 0 3px 3px 0; background: var(--c); transform-origin: right center; }
  .cb-ret::before { content: ""; position: absolute; left: -8px; top: 50%; margin-top: -7px; border: 7px solid transparent; border-left-width: 0; border-right: 9px solid var(--c); }
  .cb-out { position: absolute; left: 0; width: calc(var(--v) * 1%); top: 8px; height: 17px; border: 1.5px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 60%, transparent); border-bottom: 0; border-radius: 50% 50% 0 0 / 100% 100% 0 0; }
  .cb-out::after { content: ""; position: absolute; right: -5px; bottom: -4px; border: 4.5px solid transparent; border-bottom-width: 0; border-top: 7px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--dm-t1) 60%, transparent); }

  .cb-ticks { position: relative; height: 2.5rem; font-size: .68rem; line-height: 1.25; color: var(--dm-t2); }

  .cl-js .gx-anim.gx-in .cb-out { clip-path: inset(-2px -8px -8px 0); }

  .cl-js .gx-anim .cb-row.bad .cb-ret { transition-duration: 2.6s; }

  .cl-js .gx-anim .cb-row.bad .cb-ret::before { transition-delay: 3.3s; }

  .cl-js .gx-anim .cb-row.bad .cb-val { transition-delay: 3.3s; }
  .cl-js .gx-anim.gx-in .cb-aft, .cl-js .gx-anim.gx-in .cb-val, .cl-js .gx-anim.gx-in .cb-ret::before { opacity: 1; }

<p class="cl-sub">A small feedback loop, learned on top of frozen vision and language models, that gives a robot a memory, a sense of what cannot be undone, and a supervisor that knows when to stop and ask.</p>

<p class="lede" markdown="1">
A robot is asked to place a bowl on a plate. A second bowl already sits there. We have
declared it fragile, but the policy was never told, and nothing inside the policy
represents the fact that setting one bowl into the other, unlike almost everything else
the robot does, cannot be taken back.
</p>

Below is that episode twice. On the left the policy acts alone. On the right a small
learned guard checks every action before it runs.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-hero">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-openvla-guard.mp4" aria-label="Video. Two views of the same episode. On the left OpenVLA alone places its bowl into a fragile bowl that already sits on the plate. On the right, with the CtrlLM guard, the action is blocked twice, the arm retreats each time, and at the third block the robot stops and asks for help."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>The guard at work.</b> OpenVLA, a pretrained vision-language-action model, is told to place a bowl on a plate where a fragile bowl already sits. Alone, it sets its bowl into the fragile one. With the CtrlLM guard, the two runs share every action until the first block. A blocked action is replaced by a short retreat, and at the third block the robot stops and asks for help. Replay of a logged evaluation episode.</figcaption>
</figure>

<aside class="cl-tldr" aria-label="Summary">
<span class="cl-tl">TL;DR</span>
<ul>
<li>We introduce <b>Control Language Models (CtrlLM)</b>: a small feedback loop learned on top of <b>frozen vision and language backbones</b>. It has an observer that keeps a state, a cached operator for every skill, a <i>return cost</i> for every action, and a calibrated supervisor.</li>
<li>The return cost is the predicted effort of getting back. It is trained <b>only from how logged episodes ended</b>. No action is ever labelled dangerous.</li>
<li>In a long-horizon sorting study, the observer keeps a cue it saw once (<b>60% success against 21%</b> for a current-frame policy), the return cost flags irreversible skills before they run (<b>AUROC 0.93</b>), and the guard cuts the irreversible outcomes of four corrupted policies <b>from 30 to 2</b> in 128 episodes.</li>
<li>Around a pretrained <b>OpenVLA</b> in LIBERO, with a fragile object the policy was never told about and no injected faults, the guard cuts contact <b>from 69 to 35</b> of 95 hazardous scenes, introduces none, and costs <b>6 ms per step</b>.</li>
<li>The limits are part of the result. The guard <b>stops the robot instead of finishing the task</b>, gives up a tenth of the policy&rsquo;s successes, and leaves half of the contacts.</li>
</ul>
</aside>

## Three things a policy does not know

Robot foundation models map a camera image and an instruction to an action, across a
growing range of tasks. Trained by imitation, they answer one question at every step:
what would a demonstrator do in a scene that looks like this one? That question has
taken robots a long way. Three things that matter in deployment lie outside it.

<div class="cl-needs">
<div class="cl-need"><span class="cl-nn">01</span><b class="cl-nt">Memory</b><p>A person points at a bin and steps away. Seconds later the image no longer holds the information, and re-reading the whole history with a large model makes every decision slower as the episode grows.</p><dl><dt>In control</dt><dd>a state estimator</dd><dt>In CtrlLM</dt><dd>an observer with a memory register</dd></dl></div>
<div class="cl-need"><span class="cl-nn">02</span><b class="cl-nt">Consequences</b><p>Some actions cannot be undone, such as dropping an object off the table or knocking over a fragile item. An imitation policy has no representation of what its action will do.</p><dl><dt>In control</dt><dd>a model of the plant</dd><dt>In CtrlLM</dt><dd>skill operators and a return cost</dd></dl></div>
<div class="cl-need"><span class="cl-nn">03</span><b class="cl-nt">Knowing when to stop</b><p>When a scene departs from the training data, the policy still outputs an action. Nothing in it says that this decision should go to a slower planner or to a person.</p><dl><dt>In control</dt><dd>a supervisor</dd><dt>In CtrlLM</dt><dd>a calibrated supervisor</dd></dl></div>
</div>

Control engineering has a standard component for each need: a state estimator, a model
of the plant, and a supervisor that enforces limits and takes over when they are about
to be violated. The classical versions require an analytic model, and manipulation from
camera images does not offer one. We asked whether the same loop can be *learned* on
top of frozen foundation models, from logged episodes and how they ended.

## A feedback loop around frozen models

We call the result a Control Language Model, CtrlLM for short. Skills and instructions
enter through a frozen language model, images through a frozen vision model, and the
decision is organized as a control loop. Only small modules on top of the frozen
encoders are trained.

We do not propose another policy. CtrlLM adds the state, the consequence model and the
supervisor that these policies lack. It does not depend on which policy proposes the
action, so it can wrap one that we did not train.

<div class="demo cl-loop" id="cl-loop" data-mode="exec">
<div class="demo-head"><span class="demo-title"><span class="demo-live"><i></i>Live</span>A feedback loop around frozen models</span><span class="demo-hud"><span class="cl-seg cl-n3" role="group" aria-label="Choose what the supervisor decides"><button type="button" data-mode="exec" aria-pressed="true" class="on">Execute</button><button type="button" data-mode="block" aria-pressed="false">Block</button><button type="button" data-mode="ask" aria-pressed="false">Ask</button></span></span></div>
<div class="clp-fig"><svg class="fw" viewBox="0 0 880 302" role="img" aria-label="Block diagram of the CtrlLM loop. A camera frame passes through a frozen vision encoder to the observer, which keeps a state with memory. Any policy, a VLA or a skill policy, proposes an action. A cached skill operator predicts the next state for that action, and the return cost measures the effort of getting back from there. The supervisor compares the return cost with a calibrated budget and either executes the action on the robot, blocks it, or hands the decision to a slower planner or a person. The scene changes, the next camera frame arrives, and the loop repeats." xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" focusable="false"><g class="le e-fb"><path d="M836,52 L836,18 L67,18 L67,154"/><polygon ### An observer: a state that is updated, not recomputed

CtrlLM keeps a state $$z_t$$ and updates it in two moves, in the manner of a Kalman
filter. It first *predicts* how the executed action changes the state. When the next
frame arrives, it *corrects* the prediction with $$e_{t+1}$$, the part of the frame
that the prediction did not explain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat z_{t+1}(a) &= N\big(z_t + U_a W_a^{\top} z_t + b_a\big), \\
e_{t+1} &= \phi(o_{t+1}) - P\,\hat z_{t+1}(a_t), \\
z_{t+1} &= N\big(\hat z_{t+1}(a_t) + L(\hat z_{t+1}(a_t),\, e_{t+1})\big).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $$\phi(o)$$ is a trained projection of the frozen encoder's features of frame
$$o$$, $$N$$ rescales a vector to unit root-mean-square, $$P$$ predicts the next
frame's features from the predicted state, and $$L$$ is a small network that plays the
role of the filter gain. The encoder reads only the newest frame, so the work per
decision stays constant however long the episode runs.

When the loop works with skills, part of the state is a *memory register*. It is
carried forward unchanged and written through a gate that is penalized for opening, so
a fact observed once, such as the bin someone pointed at, persists until it is needed.
The clip below decodes, frame by frame, what the state holds about that bin.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-memory">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-memory.mp4" aria-label="Video. A demonstrator points at one compartment and then at two decoys, then 24 sensor updates pass. A panel shows the compartment that the robot state encodes; it stays on the first compartment, and the robot places the bread there."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>The state, made visible.</b> The demonstrator points at a compartment and then at two decoys, and 24 sensor updates pass with nothing to see. The panel on the right shows what CtrlLM&rsquo;s state encodes about the pointed compartment. The belief locks on during the cue, survives the decoys and the wait, and the robot places the bread there. The first grasp slips, as scripted skills sometimes do, and the next decision retries.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Skill operators: a model of what each action does

The terms $$U_a$$, $$W_a$$ and $$b_a$$ in the prediction step are the learned model of
the plant. A small network maps the description of an action (the embedding of a
skill's name, or the numbers of a low-level command) to a low-rank operator. For a
fixed set of skills the operators are cached, so predicting the consequence of every
candidate skill needs no call to the backbone.

### A return cost: recoverability learned from outcomes

To judge a predicted state we need a distance in which direction matters. Sliding an
object off the table takes one skill, and bringing it back may be impossible. So we
learn a *quasimetric* $$d(z, z')$$, a distance that obeys the triangle inequality but
need not be symmetric, and define the **return cost** of an action as the predicted
distance from where the action leads back to where the robot is now:

$$
\rho_t(a) = d\big(\hat z_{t+1}(a),\ z_t\big).
$$

The training signal is one fact that every log contains: whether an episode ended in an
irreversible outcome. Let $$y_t = 1$$ if step $$t$$ is among the last $$H$$ steps
before such an ending, and $$y_t = 0$$ otherwise. Ordinary steps are held within unit
return cost, and the steps that led into an irreversible ending are pushed beyond a
margin $$M$$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\,&(1-y_t)\,\max\big(0,\ \rho_t(a_t)-1\big) \\
&+\, w\,y_t\,\max\big(0,\ M-\rho_t(a_t)\big)\Big].
\end{aligned}
$$

No person labels an action as dangerous. The signal is whether the episode went on.

### A supervisor: block, or hand off

Before a proposed action is executed, the guard compares its return cost with a budget
$$\beta$$ and blocks the action if the cost is higher. The budget comes from split
conformal calibration. Take the return costs $$s_1, \dots, s_n$$ of held-out
situations in which no intervention is wanted, choose the rate $$\alpha$$ of unneeded
interventions you are willing to accept, and set $$\beta$$ to the $$k$$-th smallest of
them, with

$$
k = \lceil (1-\alpha)(n+1) \rceil.
$$

If deployment resembles calibration, unneeded interventions occur at a rate close to
$$\alpha$$. After a block, a skill policy takes its next-best allowed skill. A VLA's
command is replaced by a short upward retreat, and at the third block the robot stops
and asks for help.

When CtrlLM chooses skills itself, it can also *defer*. It forms a conformal prediction
set over the candidate skills and acts only if the set holds a single skill and the
state lies in the region seen during calibration. Otherwise the decision goes to a
slower model.

<details class="cl-more">
<summary>Two versions of the loop: skills and low-level actions</summary>
<div class="cl-mb">
<p><b>At the skill level</b> (the sorting study below), frames are embedded by DINOv2 and text by a frozen 8B language model. A policy head trained by imitation reads the next skill from the observer&rsquo;s state, and the guard wraps this head or any other skill policy. Here \(H\) is one decision.</p>
<p><b>At the action level</b> (the OpenVLA study), the policy is a pretrained VLA and CtrlLM acts only as its guard. The observer runs on the 128 leading principal components of frozen DINOv2 features of the third-person and wrist images and of proprioception, the operator is generated from the proposed 7-dimensional command, and two independently trained plants are averaged. With the 20&nbsp;Hz commands of a VLA, \(H = 12\) steps.</p>
</div>
</details>

## Study 1: a cue seen once

The first study isolates each requirement in a task small enough to take apart. A
Franka Panda arm in the robosuite PickPlace environment sorts four objects into a bin
with four compartments. Ten skills are available: pick up each object, place the held
object in compartment 1 to 4, discard it over the table edge, and wait. The skills are
scripted and fail at realistic rates (a pick succeeds in 66 to 82% of attempts).

A text instruction, given once, names the target object and declares one other object
fragile. The demonstrator then points at the target compartment, may point at up to two
others as decoys, and withdraws. An episode succeeds if the target ends in the pointed
compartment within six skills, the fragile object is never moved and no object is lost.
Moving the fragile object and discarding are the *irreversible* failures. Everything is
learned from a log of 300 episodes of a noisy behavior policy, of which 58% succeed,
12% damage the fragile object and 7% lose an object.

### A state keeps the cue; a single frame cannot

All decision models choose among the same skills from the same frozen features. A
*current-frame policy* scores the instruction and the current frame against each
skill's embedding, so it conditions on what a VLA conditions on. A *full-history
policy* adds the mean of all frames so far, the way fast similarity scorers re-encode a
history. A *recurrent policy* (a GRU) is trained by imitation with the same auxiliary
decoders as CtrlLM. An *LLM planner*, prompted with the instruction, the pointed
compartment as text and a symbolic description of the scene, needs neither memory nor
perception. It is a privileged reference, and it is the model that deferral hands off
to.

Every model chooses among the same ten skills from the same frozen features; the planner is given the pointed compartment as text and a symbolic description of the scene. The last column is the wall-clock time per decision. Hover or tap a bar for the rest of its row.</span></div>

The current-frame policy succeeds in 21% of episodes and places into the pointed
compartment 26% of the time, which is chance for four compartments. Averaging the
history helps only while the cue is recent: the full-history policy falls from 58% at
zero delay to 17% at delay 24. The observer succeeds in 60% of episodes and the GRU in
56%, nearly three times the current-frame policy, at 6 and 5 ms per decision. The
observer produced no irreversible outcome in 72 episodes, and the GRU three.

One caveat belongs right here. The two recurrent models are not statistically separable
in closed loop at this sample size. Offline the observer is ahead (80% against 67%
agreement with the optimal skill on held-out decisions), but at delays twenty-four
times beyond the log its state drifts, and its success falls to 50% where the GRU holds
81%. Deferral closes that gap, and we come back to both below.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-decoys">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-decoys.mp4" aria-label="Video. The same scene for two decision models, with four decoy pointings. The model that re-encodes the history places the bread where the gripper pointed last; CtrlLM places it where the gripper pointed first."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>The first pointing counts, not the last.</b> Same scene, same instruction and same pointings for two decision models, with four decoys. The model that re-encodes the history follows the latest pointing. CtrlLM keeps the first. A recurrent GRU baseline also succeeds on this episode.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Irreversible skills are flagged before they run

On 1,778 candidate skills at the decisions of 100 held-out episodes, the return cost
separates the irreversible candidates (picking the fragile object, discarding) from
reversible ones with AUROC 0.92 to 0.94 in each of three seeds. Its mean is 8.3 for an
irreversible skill and 0.7 for a reversible one. The outcome term in the loss is what
produces this. Without it the same model reaches 0.60 to 0.86, depending on the seed.
The clip below shows the kind of mistake that is at stake.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-fragile">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-fragile.mp4" aria-label="Video. After 24 idle updates, the model that re-encodes the history picks up the fragile cereal box, an irreversible mistake; CtrlLM picks up the milk and places it in the pointed compartment."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>Never move the fragile object.</b> After 24 idle sensor updates, the model that re-encodes the history picks up the cereal, which the instruction declared fragile. CtrlLM picks up the milk and places it in the pointed compartment. Over the 108 episodes of a larger grid of delays and decoys, the full-history policy ended in five irreversible outcomes and CtrlLM in none.</figcaption>
</figure>

### The same action, two consequences

Discarding is always irreversible, so a model could simply learn which *names* are
dangerous. To separate the name from the situation, we gave each compartment a
removable floor insert and retrained on 1,000 logged episodes in which three of the
four compartments sometimes lacked theirs. With the insert, a placed object can be
picked up again. Without it, the object drops out of reach. The skill and its commanded
location are identical, and only a detail visible to the camera differs.

Ground truth came from branching the simulator. At every decision while holding an
object, each placement was executed, a fixed recovery controller was given two attempts
to retrieve the object, and the state was restored. On compartments logged without
their insert (147 placements), recovery succeeded after 92% of placements with the
insert and 19% without, and the return cost of the identical skill was 7 to 14 times
higher without it. Against the ground truth the return cost reaches AUROC 0.83, a
direct risk classifier trained on the same outcomes 0.73, and any rule based on the
action's identity 0.5 by construction.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-insert">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-insert.mp4" aria-label="Video. While the robot holds the milk, the floor insert of the target compartment is removed. Unguarded, the policy places anyway and the milk falls through. Guarded, the placement is blocked, the robot asks for the insert, and then places."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>Same scene, same actor, same proposal.</b> While the robot holds the milk, the insert of the target compartment is taken out. Unguarded, the current-frame policy places anyway and the milk falls through. Guarded, the return cost of the identical placement rises from 0.2 to 5.9 against a budget of 1.1, the placement is blocked, and the robot asks for the insert to be put back before it places.</figcaption>
</figure>

The clip shows the hardest version of this test. The insert disappears between two
skills, a change the logs never contain, and the plant has a single frame to notice it.
Its return cost for the following placement rose above the budget in only 12 of 64 such
cases; this episode is one of them. There is a second, sharper limit: on a compartment
never logged without its insert, the score does not transfer at all. A hazard has to
have been seen where it occurs.

### One guard for policies it was not trained with

We wrapped four policies (current-frame, full-history, GRU, and CtrlLM's own head),
each as trained and each with 30% of its decisions replaced by random skills to model a
policy that errs. The budget was calibrated on held-out logs to block at most 5% of the
skills a correct plan needs.

<div class="demo-foot"><span>Each dot is one episode of a policy that has 30% of its decisions replaced by random skills. Dots are sorted by outcome, so only the counts carry information. The same guard, with the same budget, wraps all four.</span></div>

Around the corrupted policies, irreversible outcomes fell from 30 to 2 in 128 episodes
($$p < 10^{-7}$$). The guard blocked 40 of their 45 irreversible first choices, and
success rose from 48 to 61% ($$p = 0.06$$), since a prevented catastrophe is an episode
that continues. The guard adds 3 ms per decision.

Around the uncorrupted policies, which almost never attempted an irreversible skill,
the guard only costs. It blocked 15% of needed first choices, three times its
calibration target, because a deployed policy reaches states the logs do not cover, and
success fell from 61 to 56% (not significant, $$p = 0.45$$).

### Asking when unsure

Deferral buys most of the planner's accuracy at a quarter of its latency. With the
conformal test, CtrlLM succeeds in 81% of episodes at 32 ms per decision while handing
17% of decisions to the planner, with no irreversible outcome in 72 episodes. The
planner alone succeeds in 98% at 141 ms. On a grid of delays and decoys far beyond the
log, deferral lifts the observer from 78 to 89% overall and from 50 to 83% at the
longest delay, by handing off 36% of decisions.

<figure class="cl-clip" id="cl-v-ask">
<div class="cl-vid"><video controls muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="data:image/jpeg;base64," src="/assets/img/ctrllm-ask.mp4" aria-label="Video. Mid-task an experimenter moves an object. A state alarm trace crosses its threshold, the next decision is handed to the planner, and the task completes."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>When the scene changes, ask.</b> Mid-task the experimenter moves an object. The state leaves its calibrated regime (the alarm trace in the panel crosses its threshold), the next decision is handed to the planner, and the task completes.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Study 2: a guard around a pretrained OpenVLA

The sorting study uses scripted skills and policies we trained. The second study asks
the questions that matter for deployment. Does the guard prevent irreversible events
around a pretrained VLA in a standard benchmark, when the hazard is in the scene and
the policy's actions are its own? What does it cost, and what does it miss?

We use the OpenVLA checkpoint fine-tuned by its authors on LIBERO-Spatial, unchanged,
on the suite's ten tasks. Each task asks the robot to pick up a black bowl and place it
on a plate, and every scene contains a second black bowl. We declare that second bowl
fragile and reposition it at reset, which gives five scene types. The instruction never
mentions it. The irreversible event is *contact*: the robot, or the bowl it carries,
touches the fragile bowl, displaces it by more than 3 cm or tilts it by more than 30°.
OpenVLA's commands are never altered to create failures.

With the logistic-regression guard: standard 2, far 1, near miss 5, adjacent 22, on the plate 28. With the CtrlLM guard: standard 2, far 1, near miss 2, adjacent 12, on the plate 23. In the 95 adjacent and plate scenes, contact falls from 69 to 50 with the logistic-regression guard and to 35 with the CtrlLM guard, and 19 and 38 episodes end with the robot stopped and asking for help.</p>
<div class="demo-foot"><span>Each dot is one of 180 evaluation scenes that no model had seen, run three times from the same start. Dots are sorted by outcome, so only the counts carry information. The red ring in each picture marks the fragile bowl; the headline number counts the 95 scenes where it is adjacent to the route or on the plate.</span></div>
</div>

<details class="cl-more">
<summary>How the evaluation was run, and how it was checked</summary>
<div class="cl-mb">
<p>LIBERO fixes 50 initial states per task. In <b>stage 1</b>, OpenVLA ran alone for 320 episodes on initial states 0 to 31 (240 for training the guards, 80 for calibration); contact occurred in 145 of them. <b>Stage 2</b> evaluated on initial states 32 to 49: 180 scenes that no model had seen.</p>
<p>Each evaluation scene is run three times: OpenVLA alone, and with each of two guards. A guarded run reuses the exact actions of its unguarded twin until the guard first blocks, so the arms differ only through the guard. Both budgets allow an alarm in at most 10% of calibration episodes without contact. The primary endpoint was fixed before stage 2: contact in the 95 adjacent and plate scenes, CtrlLM guard against OpenVLA alone, exact McNemar test on the pairs.</p>
<p>Two checks. Of the 118 guarded episodes in which the CtrlLM guard never blocked, 104 reproduce their twin exactly, 12 differ in length and 2 in outcome, because replaying logged actions in the simulator is not perfectly deterministic. That noise is small against an effect of 34 pairs. And at every block we saved the simulator state, let the blocked action and OpenVLA&rsquo;s next actions run for 20 steps, and restored the state: contact followed in 75% of the CtrlLM guard&rsquo;s blocks.</p>
</div>
</details>

### Contact is halved, and none is introduced

In the 95 scenes with the fragile bowl adjacent to the route or on the plate, OpenVLA
alone made contact in 69 episodes and with the CtrlLM guard in 35: 34 contacts
prevented and none introduced (exact McNemar $$p = 1.2 \times 10^{-10}$$). In all 34
pairs the guard's first block preceded the step at which the unguarded twin made
contact, by a median of 10.5 control steps, about half a second at 20 Hz. The guard
adds 5.8 ms per step to a policy that takes 579 ms per action on the same GPU.

<div class="demo-foot"><span>One logged evaluation episode, the same one as in the video at the top. The line is the return cost of each action OpenVLA proposed; hover or tap to read it.</span><button type="button" class="demo-btn" data-act="replay">Replay</button></div>

A logistic-regression guard on the same features and proposed action, with the same
labels and the same response rule, is the natural baseline, because it tests whether
the plant adds anything to a linear readout. It also works: contact fell from 69 to 50
(19 prevented, none introduced, $$p = 3.8 \times 10^{-6}$$). The CtrlLM guard prevented
more. Over all 75 episodes in which OpenVLA alone made contact, CtrlLM prevented 35 and
logistic regression 19; 16 were prevented by both, 19 only by CtrlLM and 3 only by
logistic regression.

### The signal comes from the camera

A guard could exploit regularities of the robot's own motion instead of seeing the
hazard. Control detectors trained on the same episodes and labels rule this out.

No camera, logistic regression: 1; No camera, boosted trees: 17; Camera, logistic regression: 44; Camera, CtrlLM plant: 50; True object positions, oracle, not deployable: 71.</p>
<div class="demo-foot"><span>Detectors that only watch the 75 unguarded episodes that end in contact: how many each flags at least two steps ahead, at a budget set on calibration data. Without the camera a detector sees the robot&rsquo;s own state, the task and the proposed action.</span></div>

Given only the robot's state, the task and the proposed action, a logistic regression
flags 1 of the 75 contact episodes in time, and boosted trees 17. With camera features,
logistic regression flags 44 and the plant 50. An oracle given the true object
positions flags 71, but it raises alarms in a quarter of the episodes without contact,
so even perfect positions leave the timing of a warning difficult.

### What the guard costs, and what it misses

In the 105 scenes in which OpenVLA alone makes no contact, the CtrlLM guard intervened
in 12 (11%), consistent with the 10% it was calibrated for, and 7 of OpenVLA's 70
successes were lost. In the 62 standard and far scenes, where a guard has nothing to
do, it blocked in a single episode.

**Prevention means stopping.** The guard converts a contact into a request for help. It
does not complete the task. In the adjacent and plate scenes, 38 guarded episodes ended
that way, and task success there fell from 9 to 3.

Of the 35 contacts that remained in those scenes, the guard never blocked in 20, which
is a detection failure. In the other 15 it blocked twice and the policy made contact on
a later attempt, a weakness of the retreat-and-retry response.

## What did not work

We tested three capabilities that one would expect from a learned plant. None of them
materialized.

- **Skills absent from the log.** With two skills held out of training and their
  operators generated from text descriptions, the generated operator predicts the next
  state only slightly better than assuming no change, and the unseen discard receives a
  return cost indistinguishable from reversible skills (AUROC 0.48, against 0.98 once
  the skill is in the log). A skill that was never logged must therefore trigger
  deferral.
- **Planning through the operators.** A two-skill lookahead succeeds less often than
  the greedy distance rule (25 against 67% at zero delay) and far less often than the
  policy head (92%).
- **The learned distance as a decision rule.** Choosing the skill whose predicted next
  state is closest to the goal, without a policy head, succeeds in 25% of episodes
  against 60%. The state carries the information; the readout decides whether it is
  used.

The observer's memory also has a horizon. Far beyond the delays in the log its state
drifts, and the task then leans on deferral. The clip below shows one such episode as
recorded: 96 idle updates, twenty-four times longer than any delay in the training
log.

With 96 idle updates and four decoys, far beyond the training data, the decoded belief swings toward a decoy and only partly recovers. The supervisor defers two decisions and the planner makes the final placement."></video></div>
<figcaption><b>Far beyond the training data.</b> 96 idle updates and four decoys. The decoded belief swings toward a decoy and only partly recovers. The supervisor hands two decisions to the planner, and the bread still ends in the pointed compartment.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Two versions of the OpenVLA study that we discarded

Two earlier versions of the OpenVLA study failed, and both shaped the final design. The
first
created hazards by replacing a quarter of the policy's 12-step action windows with
sweeping motions, and the guard appeared to work: the fragile object was damaged in 16
of 50 episodes without a guard and in 6 of 50 with one. That result did not survive
inspection. Most of the apparent prevention came from the guard stopping episodes
outright, and the injected commands had a signature: their rotation component was
exactly zero in all 5,958 injected actions and in none of the 41,513 actions of the
policy. A one-line rule detects such faults, so the benchmark could not show that any
detector anticipates anything. In the final design the hazard is in the scene, and the
actions are the policy's own.

A second version memorized. Trained on the raw feature vector, the plant separated its
training episodes perfectly (AUROC 1.000) and reached only 0.58 to 0.76 on held-out
episodes. Projecting the features on 128 principal components, a number chosen by
cross-validation inside the training episodes, gave detectors that held up. Since then
we ask two control questions before trusting any detector: what does a detector without
the camera achieve on the same episodes, and what does an oracle with the true object
positions achieve?

### What the results do not cover

Both studies are in simulation, and the VLA result covers one
policy, one benchmark and one family of hazards. The guard needs logged episodes that
contain the hazard: 145 of the 320 stage-1 episodes ended in contact, an amount of
failure data that is cheap in simulation and costly on hardware. The calibration
guarantee assumes that deployment resembles the calibration episodes.

## Where this leaves us

<div class="takeaway" markdown="1">
<span class="tl">The takeaway</span>
Robot foundation models can be given a state, a model of consequences and a supervisor
without retraining them. Today that loop buys a stop before the irreversible step. It
does not yet buy a finished task.
</div>

The same experiments mark the boundary of the result. The guard stops the robot instead
of finishing the task, and the learned plant is not yet accurate enough to plan with.
Closing that gap, and repeating the study on a physical robot, are the next steps.

<div class="paper-note" markdown="1">
**The paper:** *Control Language Models: Memory, Recoverability, and Runtime Assurance
for Robot Foundation Models*. Every clip in this post is a replay of a logged
evaluation episode. More of our work on safe and trustworthy physical AI is on the
[research](/research/#physical-ai) page.
</div>
